blocks.p: To be brief: when the town had got over its fright, and the prisoners had recovered themselves a little, they took some heart and thought of petitioning the Prince for life again. So they drew up a third petition, and its contents were these:
Prince Emmanuel the Great, Lord of all worlds, and Master of mercy:

We, your poor, wretched, miserable, dying town of Mansoul, confess to your great and glorious Majesty that we have sinned against your Father and you, and are no longer worthy to be called your Mansoul, but rather to be cast into the pit. If you kill us, we have deserved it. If you condemn us to the deep, we can only say that you are righteous. We cannot complain, whatever you do, or however you deal with us. But oh, let mercy reign, and let it reach out to us! Oh, let mercy take hold of us and free us from our transgressions, and we will sing of your mercy and of your judgment. Amen.

This petition was to be sent to the Prince like the first. But who should carry it? That was the question. Some said, “Let the man who took the first one do it”; but others thought not, because he had fared no better. Now there was an old man in the town named Mr. Good-Deed, a man who bore only the name, but had nothing of the nature of the thing. Some were for sending him; but the Recorder was entirely against it.

“For,” he said, “we now stand in need of mercy, and are pleading for mercy; so to send our petition by a man of this name will seem to contradict the petition itself. Should we make Mr. Good-Deed our messenger, when our petition cries for mercy?

“Besides,” said the old gentleman, “suppose the Prince, as he receives the petition, should ask him, ‘What is your name?’ as for all anyone knows he may; and suppose he should answer, ‘Old Good-Deed.’ What do you think Emmanuel would say but this: ‘So! Is old Good-Deed still alive in Mansoul? Then let old Good-Deed save you from your distresses.’ And if he says that, I am sure we are lost; nor could a thousand old Good-Deeds save Mansoul.”

When the Recorder had given his reasons, the rest of the prisoners and the chief men of Mansoul opposed it too; so old Good-Deed was set aside, and they agreed to send Mr. Desires-awake again. So they sent for him and asked him to go a second time to the Prince, and he readily said he would. But they charged him to take care, whatever he did, to give the Prince no offense by any word or bearing. “For by doing that, for all we can tell, you may bring Mansoul to utter destruction,” they said.

Now when Mr. Desires-awake saw that he must go on this errand, he begged them to allow Mr. Wet-Eyes to go with him. This Mr. Wet-Eyes was a near neighbor of Mr. Desires, a poor man, a man of a broken spirit, yet one who could speak well in support of a petition. So they agreed that he should go with him. Then they set about their business: Mr. Desires put a rope around his head, and Mr. Wet-Eyes went wringing his hands. And so they went to the Prince’s pavilion.

Now as they went to petition this third time, they could not help thinking that by coming so often they might become a burden to the Prince. So at the door of his pavilion they first apologized for coming to trouble Emmanuel so often. They had not come, they said, because they delighted in being troublesome or liked to hear themselves talk, but because necessity drove them to his Majesty. They could have no rest day or night because of their transgressions against Shaddai and against Emmanuel, his Son. They also thought that some misbehavior of Mr. Desires-awake the last time might have displeased his Highness, and so sent him back from so merciful a Prince empty-handed and without a kind look. So when they had made this apology, Mr. Desires-awake threw himself flat on the ground, as at first, at the feet of the mighty Prince, saying, “Oh, that Mansoul might live before you!” and so he delivered his petition.

Then the Prince, having read the petition, turned aside a while as before; and coming back to the place where the petitioner lay on the ground, he asked him what his name was, and what standing he had in the eyes of Mansoul, that he, above all the multitude in Mansoul, should be sent to him on such an errand.

Then the man said to the Prince, “Oh, let not my Lord be angry. And why do you ask the name of such a dead dog as I am? Pass it by, I beg you, and take no notice of who I am, because, as you know very well, there is so great a distance between me and you. Why the townsmen chose to send me to my Lord on this errand is best known to themselves; but it could not be because they thought I had favor with my Lord. For my part, I am out of love with myself; so who else should be in love with me? Yet I want to live, and I want my townsmen to live too; and because both they and I are guilty of great transgressions, they have sent me, and I have come in their names to beg my Lord for mercy. So please incline to mercy; but do not ask what your servants are.”

Then the Prince said, “And who is this who has become your companion in so weighty a matter?” So Mr. Desires told Emmanuel that he was a poor neighbor of his, and one of his closest friends. “And his name,” he said, “if it please your most excellent Majesty, is Wet-Eyes, of the town of Mansoul. I know that there are many of that name who are worthless; but I hope it will give my Lord no offense that I have brought my poor neighbor with me.”
Then Mr. Wet-Eyes fell on his face to the ground and made this apology for coming with his neighbor to his Lord:

“O my Lord,” he said, “what I am I do not know myself, nor whether my name is false or true, especially when I begin to think of what some have said: that this name was given me because Mr. Repentance was my father. Good men have bad children, and the sincere often father hypocrites. My mother also called me by this name from the cradle; but whether because of the wetness of my brain or the softness of my heart, I cannot tell. I see dirt in my own tears, and filth at the bottom of my prayers. But I beg you (and all this while the gentleman wept) not to remember our transgressions against us, nor to take offense at how unfit your servants are, but mercifully to pass over the sin of Mansoul, and hold back no longer from glorifying your grace.”
So at his bidding they got up, and both stood trembling before him, and he spoke to them to this effect:

“The town of Mansoul has grievously rebelled against my Father, in that they rejected him as their King, and chose for their captain a liar, a murderer, and a runaway slave. For this Diabolus, your pretended prince, though you once thought so highly of him, rebelled against my Father and me, even in our palace and highest court there, thinking to become a prince and king. But he was found out in time and seized, and for his wickedness bound in chains and set apart for the pit with those who were his companions; and then he offered himself to you, and you received him.

“Now this is, and for a long time has been, a high affront to my Father; so my Father sent you a powerful army to bring you back to your obedience. But you know how you regarded these men, their captains, and their counsels, and what they received at your hands. You rebelled against them, you shut your gates on them, you gave them battle, you fought them, and you fought for Diabolus against them. So they sent to my Father for more power, and I have come with my men to subdue you. But as you treated the servants, so you treated their Lord. You stood up against me in hostility, you shut your gates against me, you turned a deaf ear to me, and you resisted as long as you could; but now I have conquered you. Did you cry to me for mercy as long as you had hopes of prevailing against me? But now that I have taken the town, you cry. Why did you not cry before, when the white flag of my mercy, the red flag of justice, and the black flag that threatened execution were set up to summon you to it? Now that I have conquered your Diabolus, you come to me for favor; but why did you not help me against the mighty? Yet I will consider your petition, and will answer it in a way that will be for my glory.

“Go, tell Captain Boanerges and Captain Conviction to bring the prisoners out to me in the camp tomorrow; and say to Captain Judgment and Captain Execution, ‘Stay in the castle, and take good care to keep everything quiet in Mansoul until you hear further from me.’” And with that he turned away from them and went back into his royal pavilion.

So the petitioners, having received this answer, set out as before to go back to their companions. But they had not gone far before the thought began to work in their minds that the Prince as yet intended no mercy for Mansoul. So they made for the place where the prisoners lay bound; but these workings of mind had such a hold on them that by the time they reached those who had sent them, they could scarcely deliver their message.

But at last they came to the gates of the town (the townsmen were waiting eagerly for their return), where many met them, wanting to know what answer the petition had received. “What news from the Prince?” they cried out to the messengers. “And what has Emmanuel said?” But the messengers said that, as before, they must go up to the prison and deliver their message there. So off they went to the prison, with a crowd at their heels. When they came to the prison gates, they told the prisoners the first part of Emmanuel’s speech: how he had dwelt on their disloyalty to his Father and himself, and how they had chosen and sided with Diabolus, had fought for him, listened to him, and been ruled by him, but had despised the Prince and his men. This made the prisoners turn pale. But the messengers went on: “The Prince also said that he would still consider your petition, and give it such an answer as would agree with his glory.” And as these words were spoken, Mr. Wet-Eyes gave a great sigh. At this they all sank into gloom and could not tell what to say; fear took hold of them in an extraordinary way, and death seemed to sit on some of their eyebrows.

Now there was in the company a notable, sharp-witted fellow, a man of small means, whose name was old Inquisitive. This man asked the petitioners whether they had told every bit of what Emmanuel said.
“Truly, no,” they answered.
“I thought so,” said Inquisitive. “Tell us, what else did he say to you?”

Then they paused a while; but at last they brought it all out. “The Prince told us to have Captain Boanerges and Captain Conviction bring the prisoners down to him tomorrow, and that Captain Judgment and Captain Execution should take charge of the castle and the town until they heard further from him.” They said also that when the Prince had given them these orders, he immediately turned his back on them and went into his royal pavilion.

But oh, how this report, and especially its last clause, that the prisoners must go out to the Prince in the camp, broke the strength of them all to pieces! With one voice they raised a cry that reached up to the heavens. This done, each of the three prepared himself to die (and the Recorder said to them, “This is the thing I feared” [Job 3:25]), for they concluded that by sundown tomorrow they would be tumbled out of the world. The whole town expected nothing else but that, each in their turn, they must all drink of the same cup. So Mansoul spent that night in mourning, in sackcloth and ashes. And when the time came for the prisoners to go down before the Prince, they dressed in mourning clothes, with ropes on their heads. The whole town also showed itself on the wall, all in mourning, in case the sight might move the Prince to compassion. But oh, how the busybodies of Mansoul bestirred themselves now! They ran here and there through the streets in companies, crying out in an uproar, one saying one thing and another the exact opposite, until Mansoul was nearly driven to distraction.

Well, the time has come for the prisoners to go down to the camp and appear before the Prince. And this was the manner of their going: Captain Boanerges went in front with a guard, Captain Conviction came behind, and the prisoners went in the middle, bound in chains. So, I say, the prisoners went in the middle, and the guard went before and behind with flying colors; but the prisoners went with drooping spirits.

Or, more particularly, like this: the prisoners went down all in mourning. They put ropes on themselves; they went along beating their breasts, but did not dare lift up their eyes to heaven. So they went out of the gate of Mansoul until they came into the middle of the Prince’s army, the sight and glory of which greatly increased their distress. Nor could they hold back any longer, but cried out aloud, “O unhappy men! O wretched men of Mansoul!” And their chains, mixing their mournful notes with the prisoners’ cries, made the noise more pitiful still.

When they came to the door of the Prince’s pavilion, they threw themselves flat on the ground; and someone went in and told his Lord that the prisoners had come. Then the Prince took his seat on a throne of state and sent for them; and when they came in, they trembled before him and covered their faces with shame. As they drew near to where he sat, they threw themselves down before him.
Then the Prince said to Captain Boanerges, “Tell the prisoners to stand up.” So they stood trembling before him, and he said, “Are you the men who were once the servants of Shaddai?”
“Yes, Lord, yes,” they said.
“Are you the men,” the Prince said again, “who let yourselves be corrupted and defiled by that abominable one, Diabolus?”
“We did more than let it happen, Lord,” they said, “for we chose it of our own accord.”
The Prince asked further, “Would you have been content for your slavery under his tyranny to go on as long as you lived?”
“Yes, Lord, yes,” said the prisoners, “for his ways were pleasing to our flesh, and we had grown strangers to a better state.”
“And when I came up against this town of Mansoul,” he said, “did you heartily wish that I might not win the victory over you?”
“Yes, Lord, yes,” they said.
“And what punishment do you think you deserve at my hand,” said the Prince, “for these and your other high and mighty sins?”
“Both death and the deep, Lord,” they said, “for we have deserved no less.”
He asked again whether they had anything to say for themselves why the sentence they confessed they deserved should not be passed on them.
“We can say nothing, Lord,” they said. “You are just, for we have sinned.”
“And what are those ropes on your heads for?” said the Prince.
“These ropes,” the prisoners answered, “are to bind us with to the place of execution, if mercy is not pleasing in your sight.”
So he asked further whether all the men in the town of Mansoul joined in this confession as they did.
“All the natives, Lord,” they answered. “But as for the Diabolonians who came into our town when the tyrant got possession of us, we can say nothing for them.”

Then the Prince commanded that a herald be called, to proclaim throughout the camp of Emmanuel, with the sound of the trumpet, that the Prince, the Son of Shaddai, had, in his Father’s name and for his Father’s glory, won a perfect conquest and victory over Mansoul; and that the prisoners should follow him and say Amen. This was done as he had commanded. And at once the music in the upper regions sounded melodiously, the captains in the camp shouted, and the soldiers sang songs of triumph to the Prince. The colors waved in the wind, and there was great joy everywhere; only it was still missing in the hearts of the men of Mansoul.

Then the Prince called for the prisoners to come and stand before him again, and they came and stood trembling. And he said to them, “The sins, trespasses, and iniquities that you, with the whole town of Mansoul, have committed from time to time against my Father and me, I have power and commandment from my Father to forgive to the town of Mansoul; and I do forgive you accordingly.” And having said this, he gave them a large and general pardon, written on parchment and sealed with seven seals, commanding my Lord Mayor, my Lord Willbewill, and Mr. Recorder to proclaim it, and have it proclaimed, throughout the whole town of Mansoul tomorrow by sunrise.
Moreover, the Prince stripped the prisoners of their mourning clothes, and gave them beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, and the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness. [Isa. 61:3]

Then he gave each of the three jewels of gold and precious stones, and took away their ropes, and put chains of gold around their necks and earrings in their ears. Now when the prisoners heard Prince Emmanuel’s gracious words, and saw all that was done for them, they very nearly fainted; for the grace, the benefit, the pardon came so suddenly, so gloriously, and so large, that they could not stand under it without staggering. Yes, my Lord Willbewill fainted outright; but the Prince stepped to him, put his everlasting arms under him, embraced him, kissed him, and told him to take heart, for everything would be done according to his word. He also kissed and embraced and smiled on the other two, Willbewill’s companions, saying, “Take these as further tokens of my love, favor, and compassion toward you; and I charge you, Mr. Recorder, to tell in the town of Mansoul what you have heard and seen.”

Then their fetters were broken to pieces before their faces and thrown into the air, and their steps were made wide beneath them. Then they fell down at the Prince’s feet and kissed his feet and wet them with tears, and they cried out with a mighty voice, “Blessed be the glory of the Lord from this place.” [Ezek. 3:12] So they were told to get up and go to the town and tell Mansoul what the Prince had done. He also commanded that someone with a pipe and drum should go and play before them all the way into the town of Mansoul. Then what they never looked for was fulfilled, and they were made to possess what they had never dreamed of.

The Prince also called for the noble Captain Credence, and commanded that he and some of his officers should march before the noblemen of Mansoul into the town with flying colors. He also charged Captain Credence that at the very time the Recorder was reading the general pardon in Mansoul, he should march in at Eye-gate with flying colors and his ten thousands at his feet, go along the high street up to the castle gates, and take possession of the castle himself until his Lord should come there. He commanded him, moreover, to tell Captain Judgment and Captain Execution to leave the stronghold to him, and to withdraw from Mansoul and return with speed to the Prince in the camp.
And now the town of Mansoul was delivered also from the terror of the first four captains and their men.
